title: Week 3 - First Post
author: axolotlgarden
selftext:
My son loves axolotls and came up with an idea for a game. I've been asking him questions, getting him to play it and taking his feedback on board as we go.

It's called Axolotl Garden and it's a cosy 3D Android game built in Godot. I've been working on it for about three weeks now. It's nowhere near ready and there's nothing to download, but I thought some people might be interested in how I'm going about building it.

It's 100% vibe coded. I use ChatGPT for concepts and Claude Code for the development, which I've also linked up to Blender for modelling. Even the music and sound effects are made using Claude.

**How the game has changed**

Initially it was just a cosy farming game where you could grow things and look after your axolotls. The more I played it though, the more I found myself thinking "so what?". There wasn't really a reason to keep playing.

It's since evolved into a game where there's an old sanctuary that needs restoring. You raise axolotls and gradually bring the sanctuary back to life, one habitat at a time. The gardening side of things is still there, but it actually serves a purpose now.

Changing something like that has a knock-on effect on pretty much everything in the game, which is where I've found documentation quite useful.

**Design documents**

I've ended up with a master design document and ten supporting documents:

* Master design – Overall vision, gameplay loop and introduction to each of the systems.
* 01 – Games and mini-games.
* 02 – Characters, axolotl species, personalities and care.
* 03 – World, buildings and locations.
* 04 – Weather, gardening, sound and environmental interactions.
* 05 – Script architecture and dependencies.
* 06 – Economy, rewards and progression.
* 07 – UI and player journey.
* 08 – Art direction, colours, models, animations and cameras.
* 09 – Roadmap and future ideas.
* 10 – Document ownership and change control.

Being a Business Analyst probably explains why I've ended up with so much documentation!

One thing I've found particularly useful is giving features a status: implemented, parked, proposed or verify. Before doing this, Claude would sometimes treat things I'd discussed as features that already existed in the game.

I also date any significant design changes so there's a record of what I've changed my mind about.

**Managing the build**

Alongside the design documents I've got a few other documents that Claude uses during development:

* Build spec – The next piece of work broken down into manageable steps.
* Current state – What's been done, what's outstanding and what Claude needs to read when starting a new session.
* Batch briefs – Requirements and acceptance criteria for each batch.
* Bug log – Defects, expected behaviour and whether fixes have been tested.
* Art and UI standards – Reference images showing what I'm trying to achieve.
* Handovers – A record of what's changed, decisions made and anything still outstanding.

The current state document has been particularly useful when starting new sessions, rather than having Claude try to work out where everything was left.

**Using multiple agents**

I've experimented quite a bit with agents and currently have the following setup:

* Producer – Takes the build spec and puts together the batch brief.
* Builder – Implements the changes and commits the work. It's the only agent allowed to modify the game code during a batch.
* Verifier – Checks the implementation, tests it and looks at performance.
* Critic – Reviews screenshots and evidence independently without seeing the builder's notes.

Any issues identified go back to the builder before being reviewed again. I've capped this at three rounds to try and keep usage under control.

The producer then writes the handover and updates the current state document.

I've also got an art director and a design reviewer, but I don't use them on every batch.

I still make the design decisions and spend time actually playing the game. Something can meet every acceptance criterion and still be incredibly boring to play, which I've discovered a few times already.

**The biggest issue I'm having is usage.**

I'm on Claude Max and still regularly hit my limits. I've recently changed how the agents work and how much documentation they read at the start of a session to try and reduce this.

I'm curious how other people are managing larger vibe-coded projects.

How are you keeping your documentation and code in sync without spending a ridiculous amount of tokens maintaining it all?

And for those of you working on bigger projects, what changes have actually made a noticeable difference to your usage?

Happy to share more about how I've set things up if anyone's interested.

comments.author: TexturelessIdea
comments.body:
> How are you keeping your documentation and code in sync without spending a ridiculous amount of tokens maintaining it all?

I think the only real way to do this is to manage the high level stuff yourself and only give Claude small focused tasks to do. I suspect a lot of your usage is getting eaten up by the producer and the critic.

I'm fairly new to using Claude myself, so I don't know my way around it completely yet. If you have some way to check which of those agents is using the most tokens, I'd love to find out if my theory on that was right.

I've been really busy this week, and my usage has been sitting at 0%, so I thought I'd burn some tokens to help you out (and I thought it'd be a nice experiment). I'm only on Pro, but I set it to Opus 5.5 with Max effort and fed it your post with the following preface.

> I've been working on a game and wanted your opinion on what I'm doing wrong, I've attached a screen shot of the game and a post I wrote for reddit with some questions at the end. I didn't get any replies on the post, so I just wanted to see if you can answer the questions instead.

Below is Claude's reply. FYI, this used 11% of my session limit and 2% of my weekly. I apparently suck at tokenmaxxing, I'll be lucky to hit 20% this week.
______________________
______________________

Short version: I don't think you're doing anything wrong so much as paying the same setup cost many times per batch. One batch can be a producer run, up to three rounds of builder → verifier → critic, then the producer again. That's as many as eleven fresh agents, each loading instructions and re-reading files before doing any real work, and each subagent's requests count against the same usage limits as your main conversation. Most of the savings come from making those runs cheaper, or making fewer of them happen.

**Keeping docs and code in sync**

The principle: each fact lives in one place, and docs only hold what the code can't tell you. For example, the master doc should link to doc 04, not summarise it.

* **Let the code and git own "what exists".** Doc 05 is the most likely to drift and the easiest to replace. Have Claude write a small script that generates it from the project (autoloads in project.godot, class_names, signals, which scenes use which scripts). It then stays in sync for free. Handovers are mostly what a good commit message should say anyway, so have the builder write them there. Keep current state to one short page that gets overwritten, not appended to.

* **Update docs from the diff, using the agent that already has the context.** The builder knows exactly what it changed, so it flips status tags (proposed → implemented) in the same commit. Nothing should re-read the codebase or the whole doc set just to update documentation.

* **Give features IDs.** Use the same ID in design docs, batch briefs, the bug log and commit messages. Updating docs becomes "grep for F-023, edit those lines" instead of reading eleven documents. You also get a traceability matrix for free, which the BA in you may enjoy.

* **Let rarely read docs lag.** Only what agents read every session (CLAUDE.md, current state) must be exactly right. Everything else can be reconciled in an occasional audit, one doc at a time on a cheaper model. Your "verify" status is already the right tool for that. Archive old handovers somewhere nothing reads by default.

**What actually moves usage**

1. **Measure before cutting.** On Max, /usage breaks down recent usage by subagent, skill, plugin and individual MCP server, with suggested fixes, over the last day or week. /context shows what's taking up space in a session. That tells you whether your recent trimming worked and which agent is actually expensive.

2. **Make round three rare.** Anthropic's own guidance warns that a reviewer told to find gaps will usually report some even when the work is sound. Chasing them all leads to over-engineering, so reviewers should flag only issues affecting correctness or the stated requirements. If your critic always finds something, most batches run to the cap. Have it label findings blocking or non-blocking. Only blocking ones go back to the builder; the rest go in the bug log for you to triage. On later rounds, re-check only what failed. Also scale the pipeline to the batch: a colour tweak doesn't need four agents.

3. **Let scripts do the deterministic checks.** Godot runs headless, so GUT or gdUnit4 tests can do much of the verifier's job without spending tokens. Filter what comes back: the docs show hooks that pre-filter logs or test output so Claude only sees the errors, cutting tens of thousands of tokens to hundreds. Godot's chatty console deserves the same treatment.

4. **Pick a model and effort level per agent.** If an agent's file doesn't name a model and Claude doesn't pass one, it falls back to your main session's model. So an Opus session can mean four Opus agents. The docs suggest Sonnet for most coding, Opus for complex reasoning, and Haiku for simple subagent tasks, and each agent can set its own effort level. Thinking is billed as output, can run to tens of thousands of tokens per request, and can't be turned off on the current models, so effort is your main dial.

5. **Resume the builder instead of spawning a new one.** By default each invocation is a brand-new instance, whereas a resumed subagent keeps its full history. Ask Claude to send fixes back to the same builder. One catch: subagents get a five-minute cache even on a subscription, while your main session gets an hour. A verify-and-critique pass usually takes longer than five minutes, so the resumed builder would re-read everything uncached. Give it a one-hour cache (below).

6. **Trim what every agent loads.**

* Custom subagents load your CLAUDE.md files at startup unless they set omitClaudeMd, which is meant for agents that get everything they need from the delegation prompt. That suits the critic, which only needs criteria and screenshots.  
* Keep CLAUDE.md under about 200 lines and move specialised instructions into skills, which only load when used.  
* Keep the art reference images out of everyone's startup reading except the critic's and art director's.  
* MCP servers can be scoped to a single agent with mcpServers, so only your modelling agent carries Blender.  
* /clear the main session between batches. Every request resends the whole conversation, so a session open all day draws usage for its full history even on a one-line question. /clear costs nothing, while /compact is itself a large request.

Items 4–6 come down to a few lines at the top of each agent file. In .claude/agents/builder.md:

    yaml
    ---
    name: builder
    description: Implements the current batch brief
    model: opus        # try sonnet for routine batches
    effort: high
    experimental:
      cacheTtl: 1h
    ---

And in .claude/agents/critic.md:

    yaml
    ---
    name: critic
    description: Reviews screenshots against the acceptance criteria
    model: sonnet
    effort: medium
    omitClaudeMd: true
    ---

**On the screenshot**: it's charming, and the axolotl face on the Wishing Tree is a lovely touch. Three quick things:

* **Lighting:** it's 6:30 pm and raining, but it's lit like a sunny lunchtime. Warmer evening light, a greyer tint in the rain and lanterns that visibly glow would do a lot of the cosy work cheaply.  
* **Coins:** if 50,000 coins is a debug wallet, make sure your son's playtests use the real economy. That "so what?" feeling is usually pacing, and you can't feel pacing with unlimited money.  
* **UI size:** on a phone, the big Pip/Book/Map buttons plus the quest card cover a lot of the scene. Round icons like your mail button would free up space.

If you repost on Reddit, put the two questions at the top, ideally in the title. At the end of a long post, many people never reach them.

comments.author: axolotlgarden
comments.body:
Thanks, bit of a long read but got through it.

So after each week I forgot to say I her Claude do review the workflow and maximize effort. So it reviews what it has done and writes back to some .MD files I have for instructions on agents and models.

So will take this into account
